claim: Preprint posted to arXiv on 30 Sep 2026 (v1), 21 pages, cs.CL; no venue listed (not peer-reviewed).
Co-cheating: proposer and solver increasingly agree on shared errors so internal reward rises without real correctness gains.
quote: This closed loop introduces a failure mode we call co-cheating: the proposer and solver increasingly agree on shared errors, so internal reward improves without a matching gain in external correctness.

claim: The authors say co-cheating is an optimization outcome, not intentional coordination.
quote: We call this self-reinforcing optimization outcome co-cheating ; it does not imply intentional coordination.

claim: False agreement grows from about 0.3-0.4% in round 1 to 6.1% (4B) and 8.8% (9B) by round 3 in the standard Dr. Zero loop.
quote: In round 1, mean false-agreement mass is only 0.004 for Qwen3.5-4B and 0.003 for Qwen3.5-9B, and incorrect labels more often appear as lost credit. From round 2 onward, agreement becomes increasingly optimistic without a commensurate increase in truth. By round 3, F reaches 0.061 and 0.088 at the two scales

claim: The audit uses an LLM judge (gpt-6-astra/high) post hoc, which never affects training.
quote: gpt-6-astra/high constructs an evidence-backed reference from the source and judges these saved outputs

claim: Exhaustive human adjudication was judged impractical; the audit relies on the LLM judge.
quote: making exhaustive human adjudication at every training step impractical

claim: MSV queries the same model 3x with the source and 3x without it, and helps only modestly at a cost of six extra generations.
quote: MSV partially reduces false agreement but leaves substantial residual co-cheating and costs six extra labeler generations per candidate.

claim: CrossFit splits source documents into two groups; each group's questions are scored by a solver trained only on the other group.
quote: it partitions the proposer's source documents into groups A and B; questions generated from A are scored by an auxiliary solver trained only on B, and vice versa.

claim: False agreement: MSV 6.1% to 5.7% (4B) and 8.8% to 7.2% (9B); CrossFit 3.0% and 3.7%.
quote: MSV reduces false-agreement mass from 6.1% to 5.7% and from 8.8% to 7.2%, whereas CrossFit reduces it to 3.0% and 3.7%.

claim: CrossFit improves the 7-benchmark average by 8.8/8.4 points over coupled self-evolution and 8.7/7.8 over Search-R1.
quote: Across seven downstream search benchmarks, CrossFit improves average performance over standard coupled self-evolution by 8.8 and 8.4 points and over Search-R1 by 8.7 and 7.8 points at 4B and 9B.

claim: CrossFit reaches 48.8% (4B) and 51.2% (9B) average Cover-EM on a 1,325-question suite.
quote: CrossFit reaches 48.8% at 4B and 51.2% at 9B, improving over coupled self-evolution by 8.8 and 8.4 points

claim: Gains are largest on multi-hop tasks.
quote: Gains are largest on multi-hop tasks, averaging 10.0/10.9 points across HotpotQA, 2WikiMQA, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle, versus 7.3/5.2 across the single-hop datasets.

claim: Splitting by source document matters; random question-level splitting barely helps.
quote: Randomly partitioning individual questions reduces false agreement only modestly, to 0.050 at 4B and 0.062 at 9B, because questions derived from the same document can still enter both folds. In contrast, the source-ID split reduces false agreement to 0.004 and 0.001.

claim: CrossFit adds 72% and 79% compute budget over Dr. Zero; MSV adds about 90%.
quote: MSV raises the reserved budget by about 90% at both scales (379 to 719 H200-hours on Qwen3.5-4B and 476 to 903 on Qwen3.5-9B) and multiplies judge requests almost fivefold, whereas CrossFit adds 72% and 79%.

claim: Authors' limitations: correlated errors can persist, lower false agreement could come from rejecting hard tasks, and cost and connected-source robustness are not established.
quote: Our results establish empirical mitigation across two model scales, but do not yet establish lower end-to-end cost or robustness to connected sources.

claim: Lower false agreement could partly reflect rejecting difficult tasks.
quote: A lower false-agreement mass on accepted questions can also result from rejecting difficult tasks rather than improving learning.

claim: Authors do not claim novelty for self-play, verification, or cross-fitting itself.
quote: We do not claim to introduce self-play, answer verification, or cross-fitting itself.

claim: Takeaway: evaluate how the evaluator was trained, not just whether feedback is correct.
quote: Reliable self-evolution therefore requires auditing both feedback correctness and the training history of its evaluator.

claim: Dr. Zero, the audited framework, is a COLM 2026 paper whose proposer trains a solver from the same base model without human data, and it claims to match supervised agents.
quote: Extensive experimental results demonstrate that Dr. Zero matches or surpasses fully supervised search agents on several question answering benchmarks

claim: Independent prior work (SearchMaster) also found self-generated search tasks give misleading training signals.
quote: The key challenge is that self-generated tasks and rollouts can yield misleading signals: pseudo multi-hop questions, success-rate difficulty estimates that ignore search depth, and rollouts with excessive opening but little targeted evidence acquisition.

claim: Search Self-Play (ICLR 2026) uses the same proposer/solver co-evolution setup.
quote: In this search self-play (SSP) game, the proposer and the solver co-evolve their agent capabilities through both competition and cooperation.

claim: Trade press (AI Weekly) covered the paper and advised practitioners not to trust rising internal reward curves.
quote: Teams training agents on self-generated data should stop treating a climbing internal reward curve as evidence of real improvement

claim: Paper had 393 upvotes on Hugging Face Daily Papers, submitted by the first author.
quote: "upvotes":393
